#Text=Cedar.
#Text=A very sweet wood, and fine timber, whereof if nests of chests be
#Text= there made, or timber thereof fitted for sweet and fine bedsteds, tables,
#Text= desks, lutes, virginals, and many things els, (of which there hath bene
#Text= proofe made already) to make vp fraight with other principall commodities,
#Text= will yeeld profit.
#Text=Wine.
#Text=There are two kindes of grapes that the soile doth yeeld naturally,
#Text= the one is small and sowre, of the ordinary bignesse as ours in England,
#Text= the other farre greater and of himselfe lushious sweet.
#Text=When they are
#Text= planted and husbanded as they ought, a principall commodity of wines by
#Text= them may be raised.
#Text=Oile.
#Text=There are two sorts of Walnuts, both holding oile; but the one farre
#Text= more plentifull then the other.
#Text=When there are mils and other deuices for
#Text= the purpose, a commodity of them may be raised, because there are infinite
#Text= store.
#Text=There are also three seuerall kindes of berries in the forme of
#Text= Oke-akornes, which also by the experience and vse of the inhabitants, we
#Text= find to yeeld very good and sweet oile.
#Text=Furthermore, the beares of the
#Text= countrey are commonly very fat, and in some places there are many.
#Text=Their
#Text=others then welwillers might be there withall acquainted, not to the good
#Text= of the action, I haue wittingly omitted them: knowing that to those that
#Text= are well disposed, I haue vttered, according to my promise and purpose,
#Text= for this part sufficient.
#Text=The second part of such commodities as Virginia is knowen to yeeld for
#Text= victuall and sustenance of mans life, vsually fed vpon by the naturall
#Text= inhabitants; as also by vs, during the time of our abode: and first of
#Text= such as are sowed and husbanded.
#Text=Pagatowr, a kinde of graine so called by the inhabitants: the same in the
#Text= West Indies is called Mayz: English men call it Guinywheat or
#Text= Turkey-wheat, according to the names of the countreys from whence the like
#Text= hath beene brought.
#Text=The graine is about the bignesse of our ordinary
#Text= English peaze, and not much different in forme and shape: but of diuers
#Text= colours: some white, some red, some yellow, and some blew.
#Text=All of them
#Text= yeeld a very white and sweet flowre: being vsed according to its kinde, it
#Text=maketh a very good bread.
#Text=We made of the same in the countrey some Mault,
#Text= whereof was brewed as good Ale as was to be desired.
#Text=So likewise by the
#Text= helpe of Hops, therof may be made as good Beere.
#Text=It is a graine of
#Text= maruellous great increase: of a thousand, fifteene hundred, and some two
#Text= thousand folde.
#Text=There are three sorts, of which two are ripe in eleuen and
#Text= twelue weeks at the most, sometimes in tenne, after the time they are set,
#Text= and are then of height in stalke about sixe or seuen foot.
#Text=The other sort
#Text= is ripe in fourteene, and is about tenne foot high, of the stalks some
#Text= beare foure heads, some three, some one, and some two: euery head
#Text= containing fiue, sixe, or seuen hundred graines, within a few more or
#Text= lesse.
#Text=Of these graines, besides bread, the inhabitants make victuall,
#Text= either by parching them, or seething them whole vntill they be broken: or
#Text= boiling the flowre with water into a pap.
#Text=Okingier, called by vs Beanes, because in greatnesse and partly in shape
#Text= they are like to the beanes in England, sauing that they are flatter, of
#Text= more diuers colours, and some pide.
#Text=The leafe also of the stemme is much
#Text= different.
#Text=In taste they are altogether as good as our English peaze.
#Text=Wickonzowr, called by vs Peaze, in respect of the Beanes, for distinction
#Text=sake, because they are much lesse, although in forme they little differ:
#Text= but in goodnesse of taste much like, and are far better then our English
#Text= Peaze.
#Text=Both the beanes and peaze are ripe in ten weeks after they are set.
#Text=They make them victuall either by boiling them all to pieces into a broth,
#Text= or boiling them whole vntill they be soft, and beginne to breake, as is
#Text= vsed in England, either by themselues, or mixtly together: sometime they
#Text= mingle of the Wheat with them: sometime also, being whole sodden, they
#Text= bruse or punne them in a morter, and thereof make loaues or lumps of
#Text= doughish bread, which they vse to eat for variety.
#Text=Macocquer, according to their seueral formes, called by vs Pompious,
#Text= Melons, and Gourds, because they are of the like formes as those in
#Text= England.
#Text=In Virginia such of seuerall formes are of one taste, and very
#Text= good, and do also spring from one seed.
#Text=There are of two sorts: one is
#Text= ripe in the space of a moneth, and the other in two moneths.
#Text=There is an herbe which in Dutch is called Melden.
#Text=Some of those that I
#Text= describe it vnto take it to be a kinde of Orage: it groweth about foure or
#Text= fiue foot high: of the seede thereof they make a thicke broth, and pottage
#Text= of a very good taste: of the stalke by burning into ashes they make a
#Text=kinde of salt earth, wherewithall many vse sometimes to season their
#Text= broths: other salt they know not.
#Text=We ourselues vsed the leaues for
#Text= pot-herbs.
#Text=There is also another great herbe, in forme of a Marigolde, about sixe
#Text= foot in height, the head with a floure is a spanne in bredth.
#Text=Some take it
#Text= to be Planta Solis: of the seeds hereof they make both a kinde of bread
#Text= and broth.
#Text=All the aforesayde commodities for victuall are set or sowed, sometimes in
#Text= grounds apart and seuerally by themselues, but for the most part together
#Text= in one ground mixtly: the maner thereof, with the dressing and preparing
#Text= of the ground, because I will note vnto you the fertility of the soile, I
#Text= thinke good briefly to describe.
#Text=The ground they neuer fatten with mucke, dung, or any other thing, neither
#Text= plow nor digge it as we in England, but onely prepare it in sort as
#Text= followeth.
#Text=A few days before they sowe or set, the men with woodden
#Text= instruments made almost in forme of mattocks or hoes with long handles:
#Text= the women with short peckers or parers, because they vse them sitting, of
#Text=growing many together one by another in ropes, as though they were
#Text= fastened with a string.
#Text=Being boiled or sodden, they are very good meat.
#Text=(M306) Monardes calleth these roots, Beads or Pater nostri of Santa
#Text= Helena.(97)
#Text=
#Text= Okeepenauk are also of round shape, found in dry grounds: some are of the
#Text= bignesse of a mans head.
#Text=They are to be eaten as they are taken out of the
#Text= ground: for by reason of their drinesse they will neither rost nor seethe.
#Text=Their taste is not so good as of the former roots: notwithstanding for
#Text= want of bread, and sometimes for variety the inhabitants vse to eat them
#Text= with fish or flesh, and in my iudgement they do as well as the housholde
#Text= bread made of Rie here in England.
#Text=Kaishucpenauk, a white kinde of roots about the bignesse of hennes egges,
#Text= and neere of that forme: their taste was not so good to our seeming as of
#Text= the other, and therefore their place and maner of growing not so much
#Text= cared for by vs: the inhabitants notwithstanding vsed to boile and eat
#Text= many.
#Text=Tsinaw, a kind of root much like vnto that which in England is called the
#Text=China root brought from the East Indies.
#Text=And we know not any thing to the
#Text= contrary but that it may be of the same kinde.
#Text=These roots grow many
#Text= together in great clusters, and do bring foorth a brier stalke, but the
#Text= leafe in shape farre vnlike: which being supported by the trees it groweth
#Text= neerest vnto, will reach or climbe to the top of the highest.
#Text=From these
#Text= roots while they be new or fresh, being chapt into small pieces, and
#Text= stampt, is strained with water a iuice that maketh bread, and also being
#Text= boiled, a very good spoonmeat in maner of a gelly, and is much better in
#Text= taste, if it be tempered with oile.
#Text=This Tsinaw is not of that sort, which
#Text= by some was caused to be brought into England for the China root; for it
#Text= was discouered since, and is in vse as is aforesayd: but that which was
#Text= brought hither is not yet knowen, neither by vs nor by the inhabitants to
#Text= serue for any vse or purpose, although the roots in shape are very like.
#Text=Coscushaw some of our company tooke to be that kinde of root which the
#Text= Spanyards in the West Indies call Cassauy, whereupon also many called it
#Text= by that name: it groweth in very muddy pooles, and moist grounds.
#Text=Being
#Text= dressed according to the countrey maner, it maketh a good bread, and also
#Text= a good spoonmeat, and is vsed very much by the inhabitants.
#Text=(M307) The
#Text= iuice of this root is poison, and therefore heed must be taken before any
#Text=thing be made therewithall: either the roots must be first sliced and
#Text= dried in the Sunne, or by the fire, and then being punned into floure,
#Text= will make good bread: or els while they are greene they are to be pared,
#Text= cut in pieces, and stampt: loaues of the same to be layd nere or ouer the
#Text= fire vntill it be sowre; and then being well punned againe, bread or
#Text= spoonmeat very good in taste and holesome may be made thereof.
#Text=Habascon is a root of hote taste, almost of the forme and bignesse of a
#Text= Parsnip: of it selfe it is no victuall, but onely a helpe, being boiled
#Text= together with other meats.
#Text=There are also Leeks, differing little from ours in England, that grow in
#Text= many places of the countrey; of which, when we came in places where they
#Text= were, we gathered and eat many, but the naturall inhabitants neuer.
#Text=Of fruits.
#Text=Chesnuts there are in diuers places great store: some they vse to eat raw,
#Text=some they stampe and boile to make spoonmeat, and with some being sodden,
#Text= they make such a maner of dough bread as they vse of their beanes before
#Text= mentioned.
#Text=Walnuts.
#Text=There are two kinds of Walnuts, and of them infinite store: in
#Text= many places where are very great woods for many miles together, the third
#Text= part of trees are Walnut trees.
#Text=The one kind is of the same taste and
#Text= forme, or little differing from ours of England, but that they are harder
#Text= and thicker shelled: the other is greater, and hath a very ragged and hard
#Text= shell: but the kernel great, very oily and sweet.
#Text=Besides their eating of
#Text= them after our ordinary maner, they breake them with stones, and punne
#Text= them in morters with water, to make a milke which they vse to put into
#Text= some sorts of their spoonemeat: also among their sodde wheat, peaze,
#Text= beanes and pompions, which maketh them haue a farre more pleasant taste.
#Text=Medlars, a kinde of very good fruit: so called by vs chiefly for these
#Text= respects: first in that they are not good vntill they be rotten, then in
#Text= that they open at the head as our Medlars, and are about the same
#Text= bignesse: otherwise in taste and colour they are farre different; for they
#Text= are as red as cheries, and very sweet: but whereas the chery is sharpe
#Text=sweet, they are lushious sweet.
#Text=(M308) Mutaquesunnauk, a kinde of pleasant fruit almost of the shape and
#Text= bignesse of English peares, but they are of a perfect red colour as well
#Text= within as without.
#Text=They grow on a plant whose leaues are very thicke, and
#Text= full of prickles as sharpe as needles.
#Text=Some that haue bene in the Indies,
#Text= where they haue seene that kind of red die of great price, which is called
#Text= Cochinile, to grow, doe describe this plant right like vnto this of
#Text= Metaquesunnauk; but whether it be the true Cochinile, or a bastard or
#Text= wilde kinde, it cannot yet be certified, seeing that also, as I heard,
#Text= Cochinile is not of the fruit, but found on the leaues of the plant: which
#Text= leaues for such matter we haue not so specially obserued.
#Text=Grapes there are of two sorts, which I mentioned in the merchantable
#Text= commodities.
#Text=Strawberries there are as good and as great as those which we haue in our
#Text= English gardens.
#Text=Mulberies, Applecrabs, Hurts or Hurtleberies, such as we haue in England.
#Text=drie vpon hurdles made of reeds, with fire vnderneath, almost after the
#Text= maner as we dry Malt in England.
#Text=When they are to be vsed, they first
#Text= water them vntill they be soft, and then being sod, they make a good
#Text= victuall, either to eat so simply, or els being also punned to make loaues
#Text= or lumps of bread.
#Text=These be also the three kinds, of which I sayd before
#Text= the inhabitants vsed to make sweet oile.
#Text=Another sort is called Sapummener, which being boiled or parched, doth eat
#Text= and taste like vnto Chesnuts.
#Text=They sometime also make bread of this sort.
#Text=The fift sort is called Mangummenauk, and is the acorne of their kinde of
#Text= Oake, the which being dried after the maner of the first sorts, and
#Text= afterward watered, they boile them, and their seruants, or sometime the
#Text= chiefe themselues, either for variety or for want of bread, do eat them
#Text= with their fish or flesh.
#Text=Of Beasts.
#Text=Deere, in some places there are great store: neere vnto the Sea coast they
#Text= are of the ordinary bignesse of ours in England, and some lesse: but
#Text= further vp into the countrey, where there is better food, they are
#Text= greater: they differ from ours onely in this, their tailes are longer, and
#Text= the snags of their hornes looke backwards.
#Text=Conies.
#Text=Those that we haue seene, and all that we can heare of are of a
#Text= gray colour like vnto Hares: in some places there are such plenty that all
#Text= the people of some townes make them mantles of the furre or flue of the
#Text= skinnes of those which they vsually take.
#Text=Saquenuckot and Maquowoc, two kinds of small beasts greater then Conies,
#Text= which are very good meat.
#Text=We neuer tooke any of them our selues, but
#Text= sometime eat of such as the inhabitants had taken and brought vnto vs.
#Text=Squirels, which are a grey colour, we haue taken and eaten.
#Text=Beares, which are of blacke colour.
#Text=The beares of this countrey are good
#Text= meat.
#Text=The inhabitants in time of Winter do vse to take and eat many: so
#Text= also sometime did we.
#Text=They are taken commonly in this sort: In some
#Text=Islands or places where they are, being hunted for assoone as they haue
#Text= spiall of a man, they presently run away, and then being chased, they
#Text= clime and get vp the next tree they can: from whence with arrowes they are
#Text= shot downe starke dead, or with those wounds that they may after easily be
#Text= killed.
#Text=We sometime shot them downe with our calieuers.
#Text=I haue the name of eight and twenty seuerall sorts of beasts, which I haue
#Text= heard of to be here and there dispersed in the countrey, especially in the
#Text= maine; of which there are onely twelue kinds that we haue yet discouered;
#Text= and of those that be good meat we know only them before mentioned.
#Text=The
#Text= inhabitants sometime kill the Lion, and eat him:(98) and we sometime as
#Text= they came to our hands of their Woolues or Wooluish dogs, which I haue not
#Text= set downe for good meat, least that some would vnderstand my iudgement
#Text= therein to be more simple then needeth, although I could alleage the
#Text= difference in taste of those kinds from ours, which by some of our company
#Text= haue bene experimented in both.
#Text=Of Fowle.
#Text=Europe, which yeeld most sweet savours farre from the shoare, the
#Text= propertie whereof we could not learne for the cause aforesayd, and not for
#Text= any difficulty to passe through the woods, seeing they are not so thicke
#Text= but that a man may passe through them.
#Text=Neither doe we thinke that they
#Text= partaking of the East world round about them, are altogether voyd of drugs
#Text= and spicery, and other riches of golde, seeing the colour of the land doth
#Text= so much argue it.
#Text=And the land is full of many beastes, as Stags, Deere
#Text= and Hares, and likewise of Lakes and Pooles of fresh water, with great
#Text= plentie of Fowles, conuenient for all kinde of pleasant game.
#Text=This land is
#Text= in latitude 34. degrees, with good and wholesome ayre, temperature,
#Text= betweene hot and colde, no vehement windes doe blowe in those Regions, and
#Text= those that doe commonly reigne in those coasts, are the Northwest and West
#Text= windes in the summer season, (in the beginning whereof we were there) the
#Text= skie cleere and faire with very little raine: and if at any time the ayre
#Text= be cloudie and mistie with the Southerne winde, immediatly it is dissolued
#Text= and waxeth cleere and fayre againe.
#Text=The Sea is calme, not boysterous, the
#Text= waues gentle: and although all the shore be somewhat sholde and without
#Text= harborough, yet it is not dangerous to the saylers, being free from rocks
#Text= and deepe, so that within 4. or 5. foote of the shore, there is 20. foote
#Text= deepe of water without ebbe or flood, the depth still increasing in such
#Text=lodged, visited, and serued of all the inhabitants of that Citie, and all
#Text= his companie had their lodgings freely: those which desired to goe into
#Text= the countrie, were diuided by foure and foure, and sixe and sixe in the
#Text= farmes or granges, according to the abilitie of the owners of the farmes,
#Text= and were furnished by them with all things necessarie.
#Text=Chap.
#Text=V.
#Text=Of the inhabitants which are in the Citie of S.
#Text=Iago, and in the
#Text= other townes of the Island: and of the qualitie of the soile, and fruites
#Text= that it yeeldeth.
#Text=The Citie of S.
#Text=Iago hath fourescore houses which are great and well
#Text= contriued.
#Text=The most part haue their walls made of bords, and are couered
#Text= with thatch; it hath some houses builded with lime and stone, and couered
#Text= with tiles.
#Text=(M603) It hath great Orchards and many trees in them,
#Text= differing from those of Spaine: there be figgetrees which beare figges as
#Text= big as ones fist, yellow within, and of small taste; and other trees which
#Text= beare a fruit which they call Ananes, in making and bignes like to a small
#Text=Pineapple: it is a fruite very sweete in taste: the shel being taken away,
#Text= the kernel is like a peece of fresh cheese.
#Text=In the granges abroad in the
#Text= countrie there are other great pineapples, which grow on low trees, and
#Text= are like the Aloe tree:(126) they are of a very good smell and exceeding
#Text= good taste.
#Text=Other trees do beare a fruit, which they call Mameis of the
#Text= bignes of Peaches.
#Text=This the Islanders do hold for the best fruit of the
#Text= country.
#Text=There is another fruit which they call Guayahas like Filberds, as
#Text= bigge as figges.
#Text=There are other trees as high as a iaueline, hauing one
#Text= only stocke without any bough, and the leaues as long as a casting dart:
#Text= and the fruite is of the bignesse and fashion of a Cucumber, one bunch
#Text= beareth 20. or 30. and as they ripen, the tree bendeth downeward with
#Text= them: they are called in this countrie Plantanos; and are of a good taste,
#Text= and ripen after they be gathered, but those are the better which ripen
#Text= vpon the tree it selfe: they beare fruite but once: and the tree being cut
#Text= downe, there spring vp others out of the but, which beare fruite the next
#Text= yeere.
#Text=(M604) There is another fruit; whereby many people are sustained,
#Text= and chiefly the slaues, which are called Batatas.
#Text=These grow now in the
#Text= Isle of Tercera, belonging to the Kingdome of Portugal, and they grow
#Text= within the earth, and are like a fruit called Iname, they haue almost the
#Text= taste of a chestnut.
#Text=(M605) The bread of this countrie is also made of
#Text=rootes which are like the Batatas.
#Text=And the stocke whereon those rootes doe
#Text= grow is like an Elder tree: they make their ground in little hillocks and
#Text= in each of them they thrust 4. or 5. stakes; and they gather the rootes a
#Text= yeere and an halfe after they set them.
#Text=If any one, thinking it is a
#Text= Batata or Potato roote, chance to eate of it neuer so little, he is in
#Text= great danger of death: which was seene by experience in a souldier, which
#Text= assone as hee had eaten a very little of one of those rootes, hee died
#Text= quicklie.
#Text=They pare these rootes and stamp them and squese them in a thing
#Text= like a presse: the iuyce that commeth from them is of an euill smell.
#Text=The
#Text= bread is of little taste and lesse substance.
#Text=Of the fruits of Spaine,
#Text= there are Figges and Oranges, and they beare fruite all the yeere, because
#Text= the soile is very ranke and fruitfull.
#Text=(M606) In this countrie are many
#Text= good horses, and there is greene grasse all the yeere.
#Text=There be many wild
#Text= oxen and hogges, whereby the people of the Island is well furnished with
#Text= flesh: Without the townes abroad in the Countrie are many fruites.
#Text=And it
#Text= happeneth sometimes that a Christian goeth out of the way and is lost 15.
#Text=or 20. daies, because of the many paths in the thicke groues that crosse
#Text= too and fro made by the oxen: and being thus lost, they sustaine them
#Text= selues with fruites and palmitos: for there be many great groues of Palme
#Text= trees through all the Island: they yeeld no other fruite that is of any
